chapters.title: Chapter 5: Carry and Cross-Asset Value Strategies

lessons.title: Cross-Asset Value: Cheap vs Expensive Across Equities, Bonds, and Commodities

body.text: Trend asks whether price has been moving. Carry asks whether you get paid to simply hold. Value asks a third, genuinely different question: relative to some fundamental anchor, is this asset cheap or expensive right now, and is it likely to drift back toward that anchor eventually? It is the one signal in this course explicitly betting on reversion rather than persistence.

children.text: This lesson generalizes value investing, familiar from single-stock equity analysis, into a systematic, cross-asset signal, applying an asset-appropriate valuation anchor to equities, fixed income, and commodities alike, then shows why value's inherent contrarianism makes it both a genuinely useful diversifier and a genuinely uncomfortable strategy to hold through.
What "Value" Means Once You Leave Equities

Equity value investing asks whether a stock's price is low relative to its earnings or fundamentals. A systematic, multi-asset version of value asks the identical structural question of every asset class, using whatever valuation anchor genuinely applies to that asset, rather than treating value as an equities-only concept.

cells: Earnings yield relative to long-run average P/E
Current P/E well below its own historical range
Real yield (nominal yield minus expected inflation) vs history
Real yield well above its own historical average
Inflation-adjusted price vs long-run trailing average
Real price well below its own long-run average
Purchasing power parity (referenced, not this course's core currency signal)
Currency trading materially below its PPP-implied fair value

children.text: Why Value Is Inherently Contrarian, and Why That's Uncomfortable

A value signal frequently points in the opposite direction to a trend signal on the same asset, buying into recent weakness, selling into recent strength, betting on reversion where trend bets on persistence. This is precisely the behaviorally hardest position to hold, adding to what looks like a losing position, or reducing what looks like a winning one, is exactly what Chapter 1's discretionary-versus-systematic lesson identified as where human judgment breaks down most under pressure. A systematic value signal does not feel the discomfort; the person overseeing it still does, which is a genuine business and psychological risk, not just a statistical one.
Equity Value in the Indian Context: Nifty's Own P/E History

A simple systematic equity value signal need not pick individual stocks at all, it can compare Nifty 50's own trailing P/E to its own long-run historical range. Nifty's trailing P/E has historically traded roughly between the mid-teens and low-20s across a full cycle, dipping toward the lower end briefly around the March 2020 trough, and spiking well above that range through 2020 into 2021, a period worth flagging carefully, since that spike reflected a genuine earnings collapse during the pandemic as much as price strength, a distortion any P/E-based value signal needs to account for rather than reading at face value.

body.text: A trailing P/E ratio can spike not because prices rose, but because earnings collapsed, exactly what happened across 2020. A naive value signal reading a high P/E as "expensive, go short" during an earnings recession would have badly misread the underlying situation. A more robust equity value signal uses a longer-run, cycle-adjusted earnings measure, or explicitly checks whether a P/E spike is being driven by the price or the earnings side of the ratio, before treating it as a genuine valuation signal.

children.text: Value in Fixed Income: Real Yields vs History

A fixed income value signal compares the current real yield, nominal G-Sec yield minus expected or trailing inflation, to its own historical average. A real yield well above its historical norm suggests bonds are cheap relative to their own history and reasonably compensated for inflation risk; a real yield well below historical norms, or negative, suggests bonds are expensive and poorly compensated. This connects directly to Chapter 2's duration lesson: a value signal telling you bonds are cheap is really telling you the market is paying an unusually generous premium for taking on duration risk right now, relative to its own past.
Value in Commodities: Price vs Long-Run Real Average

Commodity value compares a commodity's inflation-adjusted price today to its own long-run trailing real price average, on the logic that persistently high real prices eventually draw in new supply, and persistently low real prices eventually choke off production, pulling prices back toward some long-run equilibrium. This is genuinely the weakest of the three value signals here, since production costs, technology, and demand structure shift meaningfully over the kind of multi-decade horizons this reversion logic depends on, making commodity value noisier and slower than equity or bond value.

body.text: An asset can stay cheap, or expensive, for far longer than a value signal's holding period assumes, a well-known failure mode sometimes called a value trap. Value signals are a genuine, real bet on eventual reversion, not a guarantee of timely reversion, and this is doubly true for commodities, where the long-run anchor itself can drift meaningfully over the strategy's own lifetime.

children.text: Value Complements Trend and Carry Differently Again

Value fails under sustained, expensive-getting-more-expensive bull markets, precisely trend-following's best environment, and tends to earn its keep at genuine turning points, when trend is often still catching up to a reversal that has already started. This gives the multi-strategy book building toward Chapter 7 a third, genuinely distinct regime sensitivity, alongside trend's directional bias and carry's stability bias.

body.title: The Desk Split Between Two Honest Signals
body.scenario: In late 2021, a desk's trend signal on Nifty 50 remains strongly long, following the sustained rally from the 2020 lows. In the same period, the desk's equity value signal, comparing Nifty's trailing P/E to its long-run historical range, flags the market as expensive and signals a reduced or short position, after adjusting for the earnings-collapse distortion this lesson flagged.
body.prompt: Is one of these two signals simply wrong? How should a desk running both think about this disagreement?
body.modelAnswer: Neither signal is wrong on its own terms; they are answering genuinely different questions, exactly as this lesson describes. Trend is correctly reporting that price has been persistently rising and, historically, persistence tends to continue for a while. Value is correctly reporting that price has moved well above what Nifty's own long-run earnings-based history would suggest is fair, and that valuations this stretched have, historically, tended to eventually revert. Both can be true simultaneously: a market can be both trending and expensive at the same time, right up until it stops trending. A desk running both should not force them to agree, it should treat them as separate, independently risk-budgeted signals, exactly Lesson 3's advice for carry and trend disagreement, sized so that neither signal alone can dominate the book, and rely on the combination it constructs in Lesson 5 rather than manually overriding one signal with the other.

body.title: Why Value Is the Contrarian Signal in This Course
body.question: What fundamentally distinguishes a cross-asset value signal from a trend signal, based on this lesson?
options: Value only applies to equities, while trend applies to all asset classes
Value bets on eventual reversion toward a fundamental anchor, while trend bets on the persistence of recent price direction, making the two strategies fundamentally contrarian to each other
Value and trend are mathematically identical signals with different names
Value requires no historical data, while trend requires decades of price history
body.explanation: Trend and value make opposite bets on the same underlying price history: trend assumes recent direction is informative about the near future, while value assumes price will eventually revert toward some fundamental anchor. This structural difference is exactly why the two signals can, and regularly do, disagree on the same asset at the same time.

body.title: Naming Value's Classic Failure Mode
body.textWithBlank: An asset that appears cheap by a value signal but continues to underperform or fall for a long, extended period, rather than reverting toward its historical valuation anchor as the strategy assumed, is often described as a ___.
body.explanation: A value trap is value investing's classic failure mode: an asset can remain cheap, or expensive, far longer than any specific strategy's holding period or risk budget can tolerate, which is why value signals need explicit risk management rather than being trusted to revert on any particular schedule.

points: Cross-asset value generalizes equity value investing, asking whether an asset is cheap or expensive relative to an asset-appropriate fundamental anchor, expecting eventual reversion

Equities use earnings yield or P/E relative to long-run history, fixed income uses real yield relative to history, and commodities use inflation-adjusted price relative to a long-run average, though this last one is the noisiest of the three
A P/E spike can be driven by collapsing earnings rather than rising prices, exactly what happened in 2020, and a naive value signal needs to account for this before reading it at face value
Value is inherently contrarian to trend, betting on reversion rather than persistence, which makes it genuinely useful as a diversifier but behaviorally uncomfortable to hold
Value's classic failure mode, the value trap, means an asset can stay cheap or expensive far longer than a strategy's holding period assumes
Value fails in sustained bull or bear trends and tends to earn its keep at genuine turning points, giving the multi-strategy book a third, distinct regime sensitivity alongside trend and carry
